# Pitch Deck Research

## Purpose
This skill provides deep research methodology for understanding how high-quality pitch decks are structured, what investors expect, and how narrative frameworks translate into slide sequences. Every generation decision should be grounded in real pitch deck intelligence — not assumptions about what looks good.

## Why This Research Matters

The product generates presentations. If the generated decks don't match what experienced founders and designers produce manually, the product fails. This skill ensures generation is grounded in real patterns, not generic templates.

## Pitch Deck Anatomy — The Canonical Structures

### YC-Style Pitch Deck (10-12 slides)
| # | Slide Type | Purpose | Content Pattern |
|---|-----------|---------|-----------------|
| 1 | Title/Cover | First impression, brand | Company name, tagline, logo, optional visual |
| 2 | Problem | Create urgency | 1-3 pain points, ideally with data |
| 3 | Solution | Your answer | Clear value proposition, product screenshot |
| 4 | How It Works | Demystify | 3-step process or product walkthrough |
| 5 | Market Size | Show opportunity | TAM/SAM/SOM with credible sources |
| 6 | Traction | Prove momentum | Key metrics, growth chart, logos |
| 7 | Business Model | Show revenue path | Pricing, unit economics, revenue streams |
| 8 | Competition | Show awareness | Positioning matrix or comparison table |
| 9 | Team | Build confidence | Founders + key hires, relevant experience |
| 10 | Financials | Project trajectory | Revenue projections, key assumptions |
| 11 | The Ask | Be specific | Amount raising, use of funds, timeline |
| 12 | Contact/Close | Enable follow-up | Contact info, memorable closing statement |

### Series A Expansion (15-18 slides)
Adds: detailed product slides, customer case studies, go-to-market strategy, competitive moat analysis, detailed financials with cohort data, advisor/board slide.

### Product Demo Deck (8-12 slides)
Title → Problem Context → Product Overview → Feature Deep-Dives (3-4) → Integration/Workflow → Pricing → Social Proof → CTA

### Quarterly Business Review (10-15 slides)
Executive Summary → KPI Dashboard → Goal Progress → Revenue Analysis → Customer Metrics → Product Updates → Challenges → Next Quarter Plan → Resource Needs → Appendix

## Slide-Type Taxonomy

Every slide in any presentation falls into one of these functional categories:

### Narrative Slides (drive the story)
- **Opener**: Sets context, hook, stakes
- **Problem Definition**: Creates tension the audience feels
- **Solution Reveal**: Relieves the tension with your answer
- **Evidence/Proof**: Data, testimonials, case studies that build belief
- **Vision/Future**: Where this leads, the bigger picture
- **Call to Action**: What you want the audience to do next

### Data Slides (convey information)
- **Single Metric Hero**: One big number with context
- **Dashboard/Multi-Metric**: 3-6 KPIs in a grid
- **Chart/Graph**: Trend, comparison, or distribution visualization
- **Table**: Structured data comparison
- **Financial Projection**: Revenue/cost model with assumptions

### People Slides (build trust)
- **Team Grid**: Headshots + roles + 1-line credentials
- **Testimonial/Quote**: Customer or advisor endorsement
- **Logo Wall**: Customer/partner logos as social proof
- **Case Study**: Before/after story with a specific customer

### Structural Slides (organize flow)
- **Section Divider**: Marks transitions between deck sections
- **Agenda/Outline**: What's coming (rarely needed in pitch decks)
- **Appendix Header**: Signals supplementary material
- **Thank You/Contact**: Clean close with next steps

## Content Density Rules

Research from real pitch deck analysis reveals consistent patterns:

### Text Per Slide
- **Headlines**: 3-8 words maximum. Must communicate the slide's ONE idea.
- **Body text**: 15-30 words per text block. Audiences read ≤50 words per slide.
- **Bullet points**: Max 4 bullets. Each bullet ≤ 10 words.
- **Total text per slide**: Under 75 words for narrative slides, under 100 for data slides.

### The "Glance Test"
A slide must communicate its core message in under 3 seconds of looking at it. This means:
- One clear visual hierarchy (the eye goes to one place first)
- No competing elements of equal weight
- Headlines do the heavy lifting — body text is supporting detail

### Data Visualization Rules
- **One chart per slide** unless building a dashboard layout
- **Label the insight**, not just the data ("Revenue grew 3x" not "Revenue 2022-2024")
- **Minimize chart junk** — no 3D effects, minimal gridlines, direct labels over legends
- **Use color purposefully** — highlight the data point that matters, gray out context

## Narrative Frameworks for Different Deck Types

### The Investor Story Arc
**Setup** (slides 1-3): Hook → Problem → "What if..."
**Build** (slides 4-7): Solution → Proof → Market → Model
**Payoff** (slides 8-11): Traction → Team → Vision → Ask

Key principle: Every slide must earn the next slide. If the audience isn't curious about what comes next, the narrative is failing.

### The Product Pitch Arc
**Context** (slides 1-2): Who faces this problem → Current pain
**Reveal** (slides 3-5): Product walkthrough → Key features → Demo moments
**Proof** (slides 6-8): Metrics → Testimonials → Integrations
**Close** (slides 9-10): Pricing → Next steps

### The Status Update Arc
**Big Picture** (slides 1-2): Summary → KPI dashboard
**Deep Dives** (slides 3-8): Goal-by-goal progress with data
**Forward Look** (slides 9-11): Challenges → Plans → Resource needs

## What Makes a Deck Persuasive — Research Findings

### Visual Consistency Signals Quality
- Decks with consistent color usage across all slides score higher in investor recall studies
- Typography inconsistency (mixing fonts, sizes, weights arbitrarily) is the #1 "amateur" signal
- Slide-to-slide transitions should feel like pages of the same book

### Specificity Builds Credibility
- "We grew 347% YoY" beats "We grew significantly"
- "$2.1M ARR" beats "strong revenue growth"
- "47 enterprise customers including Stripe, Shopify" beats "many customers"

### Whitespace Communicates Confidence
- Crowded slides signal the presenter doesn't know what matters
- Generous margins and spacing signal editorial discipline
- The best decks feel like they have LESS on each slide than expected

### The "So What" Test
Every slide must answer: "So what? Why does this matter to the person viewing it?"
- Bad: "Our team has 50 years combined experience"
- Good: "Our team built and sold two companies in this space — we know the playbook"

## Research Procedure

When investigating pitch deck patterns for generation:

1. **Define the deck type** — What kind of presentation is being generated?
2. **Select the canonical structure** — Match to the appropriate anatomy above
3. **Apply content density rules** — Budget words and elements per slide
4. **Map the narrative arc** — Ensure slides connect in a story, not just a list
5. **Run the "Glance Test" mentally** — Will each slide communicate in 3 seconds?
6. **Check for specificity** — Replace every vague claim with a specific one
7. **Verify visual rhythm** — Alternate between text-heavy and visual-heavy slides
8. **Apply the "So What" filter** — Remove any slide that can't justify its existence
